Emergency medicine · published research

Intensive care unit stay

A blinded trial in general ICU patients found shorter average ICU stay and better mobility and strength. A separate trial in ventilated COVID-19 patients found no significant stay difference, although several diaphragm and inflammatory measures favored combined PBM and magnetic-field treatment.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A blinded trial in general ICU patients found shorter average ICU stay and better mobility and strength. A separate trial in ventilated COVID-19 patients found no significant stay difference, although several diaphragm and inflammatory measures favored combined PBM and magnetic-field treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

Two independent randomized trials examine PBM-related treatment during intensive care. One triple-blind sham-controlled trial included 60 general ICU patients. A second placebo-controlled study included 30 intubated patients with severe COVID-19 and combined PBM with a static magnetic field, so it cannot isolate the light effect. Other ICU publications about mouth sores or pressure injuries do not test ICU stay and are not included as direct evidence for this outcome.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 60-person general ICU trial, daily red and near-infrared LED treatment was associated with an average ICU stay about 30% shorter than sham treatment. Mobility scores, Medical Research Council muscle-strength scores, and handgrip strength also improved more in the PBM group. Illness-severity scores at admission were similar between groups (Neto et al. 2024).

In the 30-person COVID-19 trial, length of stay did not differ significantly between groups. The combined PBM and static magnetic-field treatment was associated with better preservation of diaphragm thickness and changes in ventilatory and inflammatory measures, including C-reactive protein. These findings concern secondary outcomes in a specific ventilated population and do not establish that PBM alone shortens ICU stay (De Marchi et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining ICU length of stay or functional recovery during intensive care was identified in this category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study directly testing ICU length of stay was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The general ICU trial used an LED array containing 635-nm red visible and 880-nm near-infrared emitters. Ten sites were treated for 90 seconds each daily, for about 15 minutes per session, until discharge. The COVID-19 trial combined PBM with a static magnetic field and used a different clinical context. The studies did not compare doses or establish one ICU protocol that applies across diagnoses.

Interpretation

The 60-person trial reports shorter average stay together with better short-term mobility and strength, while the COVID-19 study found no significant stay difference. The functional findings are distinct from the inconsistent length-of-stay result. Differences in diagnosis, co-treatment, and discharge practice matter when judging whether the results would transfer to other ICUs.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term mobility and muscle-strength improvement in general ICU patients Low for reducing ICU length of stay across ICU populations
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A blinded 60-person ICU trial found better mobility, muscle strength, and handgrip alongside a shorter average stay. A separate small COVID-19 trial found no significant length-of-stay difference and combined PBM with a magnetic field. The functional result merits replication, while the stay outcome is less consistent. Multicentre trials with common discharge criteria and recovery measures would clarify both.
